questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 32 gives the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution. Memory hook: 32 = Supreme Court remedy.

questions.question_text: Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly of India?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Rajendra Prasad was the President of the Constituent Assembly, not the Drafting Committee chairman.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Drafting Committee was set up on 29 August 1947 with Ambedkar as Chairman. B. N. Rau was the Constitutional Adviser. Memory hook: Ambedkar = Architect of the Constitution.

questions.question_text: Fundamental Duties are contained in which Part of the Constitution of India?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Part IV holds the Directive Principles, which sits right next to Part IV-A.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) as Part IV-A, containing Article 51A. Memory hook: 51A sits in IV-A.

questions.question_text: Which Article of the Constitution defines a 'Money Bill'?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Article 109 lays down the special procedure for Money Bills in the Rajya Sabha, so it is the nearest neighbouring Article.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 110 defines a Money Bill and lists the matters it may contain. Article 109 gives the procedure and Article 112 is the Annual Financial Statement. Memory hook: 110 defines, 109 procedure.

questions.question_text: President's Rule in a State is imposed under which Article of the Constitution?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Article 352 is the National Emergency provision, so students mix up the two emergencies.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 356 deals with failure of constitutional machinery in a State. Article 352 is National Emergency and Article 360 is Financial Emergency. Memory hook: 356 = State failure.

questions.question_text: Which Schedule of the Constitution lists the functional items of Panchayats?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): The Twelfth Schedule lists functions of Municipalities, the urban counterpart added by the 74th Amendment.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Eleventh Schedule, added by the 73rd Amendment (1992), lists 29 subjects for Panchayats. The Twelfth Schedule has 18 items for Municipalities. Memory hook: 11 = Village (the two 1s look like village poles).

questions.question_text: What is the minimum age required to become a member of the Rajya Sabha?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): 25 years is the minimum age for the Lok Sabha, which students confuse with the Rajya Sabha.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 84 fixes 30 years for the Rajya Sabha and 25 years for the Lok Sabha. The President must be at least 35 years old. Memory hook: Upper House, upper age: 30.

questions.question_text: The Finance Commission of India is constituted under which Article of the Constitution?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Article 275 deals with grants-in-aid to States and is closely linked to Finance Commission recommendations.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 280 provides for a Finance Commission every five years to recommend distribution of taxes between the Union and States. Memory hook: 280 = Commission.

questions.question_text: Under which Article can Parliament legislate on a State List subject in the national interest if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by two-thirds of members present and voting?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Article 250 also lets Parliament legislate on State List subjects, but during a Proclamation of Emergency, not through a Rajya Sabha resolution.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 249 allows Parliament to legislate on a State List matter for up to one year at a time after such a Rajya Sabha resolution. Article 252 is by consent of States and Article 248 is residuary powers. Memory hook: 249 = Rajya Sabha resolution.

questions.question_text: In which year was the Battle of Plassey fought?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): 1764 is the year of the Battle of Buxar, the other decisive Company victory in Bengal.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: At Plassey in 1757 Robert Clive defeated Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah, laying the base of British rule in India. Buxar (1764) confirmed it. Memory hook: Plassey 57, Buxar 64.

questions.question_text: Who founded the Maurya Empire with the guidance of Chanakya (Kautilya)?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Samudragupta belongs to the later Gupta dynasty, and the shared 'Chandragupta/Gupta' naming causes confusion.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the Nandas around 321 BCE and founded the Maurya Empire. Bindusara was his son and Ashoka his grandson. Memory hook: Chandragupta started it, Ashoka made it famous.

questions.question_text: In which year did the Jallianwala Bagh massacre take place in Amritsar?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): 1922 is the year of Chauri Chaura and the withdrawal of Non-Cooperation, which students link with Jallianwala.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: On 13 April 1919 (Baisakhi) General Dyer ordered firing on a peaceful gathering at Jallianwala Bagh. Memory hook: Rowlatt Act 1919, Jallianwala 1919.

questions.question_text: Which incident led Mahatma Gandhi to suspend the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Jallianwala Bagh (1919) came before the movement and helped trigger it, not end it.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: At Chauri Chaura (Uttar Pradesh) a mob burnt a police station, killing policemen, and Gandhi withdrew the movement over the violence. Memory hook: Chauri Chaura = movement stopped.

questions.question_text: The Dandi March (Salt March) of 1930 began from which place?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Sevagram Ashram near Wardha became Gandhi's base later, and students confuse it with his earlier ashram.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Gandhi began the march on 12 March 1930 from Sabarmati Ashram, Ahmedabad, and reached Dandi on 6 April to break the salt law. Memory hook: Sabarmati to Dandi.

questions.question_text: The First Battle of Panipat (1526) was fought between Babur and which ruler?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Rana Sanga was Babur's opponent at Khanwa (1527), the very next major battle.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, the last Delhi Sultan, at Panipat in 1526 and began Mughal rule. Hemu fought at the Second Battle of Panipat (1556). Memory hook: Panipat I = Lodi ends.

questions.question_text: The 'Great Bath', a famous structure of the Harappan civilisation, was found at which site?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Harappa gave the civilisation its name and was discovered first, so students assume the Great Bath is there.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Great Bath was part of the citadel at Mohenjodaro in present-day Sindh, Pakistan. Lothal is known for its dockyard and Kalibangan for fire altars. Memory hook: Mohenjodaro = Great Bath.

questions.question_text: The Permanent Settlement of Bengal in 1793 was introduced by which Governor-General?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Warren Hastings is linked with earlier revenue experiments such as the five-year settlement of 1772.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Lord Cornwallis fixed land revenue permanently with zamindars as owners, in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. Memory hook: Cornwallis = Permanent Settlement.

questions.question_text: Which was the first Indian state to accept the Subsidiary Alliance introduced by Lord Wellesley?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Awadh accepted the system later (1801), and students pick it as the best-known early acceptor.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Nizam of Hyderabad accepted the Subsidiary Alliance in 1798, the first state to do so. Awadh followed in 1801 and the Peshwa through the Treaty of Bassein (1802). Memory hook: Hyderabad was first in 98.

questions.question_text: Which is the longest river of India, flowing mainly within the country?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Godavari is the longest peninsular river, so it is mistaken for the longest river overall.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Ganga, about 2,525 km long, is the longest river of India. Godavari is the longest of the peninsular rivers. Memory hook: Ganga = Longest, Godavari = Longest in the South.

questions.question_text: The Tropic of Cancer passes through how many Indian states?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Students often forget one of the small north-eastern states (Tripura or Mizoram) and count 7.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: It passes through Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram. Memory hook: G-R-M-C-J-W-T-M = 8.

questions.question_text: Which is the largest continent of the world by area?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Africa is the second largest continent, so it is the most common wrong pick.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Asia covers about 44 million sq km and has the largest population. Africa is second. Memory hook: Asia first, Africa second.

questions.question_text: Which river was historically called the 'Sorrow of Bengal' because of its devastating floods?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Kosi is called the Sorrow of Bihar, a very similar title for a neighbouring state.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Damodar flooded repeatedly before dams were built under the Damodar Valley Corporation. Memory hook: Damodar = Bengal, Kosi = Bihar.

questions.question_text: The deepest known point of the world's oceans, the Challenger Deep, lies in which trench?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Tonga Trench is also in the Pacific and is the second deepest, so it is the closest confusion.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Mariana Trench in the western Pacific reaches about 11,000 m depth. Memory hook: Mariana = Maximum depth.

questions.question_text: Chilika Lake, the largest coastal lagoon in India, is located in which state?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Pulicat Lake, another large lagoon, lies on the Andhra Pradesh-Tamil Nadu border, so students confuse the two lagoons.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Chilika is a brackish water lagoon on the Odisha coast along the Bay of Bengal. Memory hook: Chilika = Odisha, Pulicat = AP/TN.

questions.question_text: Which strait separates India from Sri Lanka?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Ten Degree Channel is an Indian channel too, but it separates the Andaman Islands from the Nicobar Islands.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Palk Strait lies between Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka, joining the Bay of Bengal and the Palk Bay. Memory hook: Palk = India-Sri Lanka.

questions.question_text: Through which Himalayan pass does the River Sutlej enter India from Tibet?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Nathu La is the best-known border pass with Tibet, but it lies in Sikkim and does not carry the Sutlej.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Sutlej enters Himachal Pradesh through Shipki La. Zoji La is in Ladakh and Bomdi La in Arunachal Pradesh. Memory hook: Sutlej = Shipki La (both start with S).

questions.question_text: The Reserve Bank of India commenced operations in which year?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): 1949 is the year of RBI's nationalisation, the most common date confused with its start.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: RBI was set up under the RBI Act, 1934 and began operations on 1 April 1935. It was nationalised on 1 January 1949. Memory hook: Act 34, start 35.

questions.question_text: The headquarters of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) is located in which city?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): ADB has traditionally been headed by a Japanese president, so students wrongly place its HQ in Tokyo.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: ADB, founded in 1966, is headquartered in Mandaluyong, Metro Manila, Philippines. Beijing hosts the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank. Memory hook: ADB = Manila.

questions.question_text: The rate at which the RBI borrows money from commercial banks for the short term is called:
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Repo Rate is the rate at which RBI lends to banks, the exact opposite direction of the flow.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Under reverse repo, banks park surplus funds with RBI and earn this rate, which absorbs liquidity from the system. Memory hook: Reverse repo = RBI borrows (Reverse of Repo). (Since 2022 the Standing Deposit Facility is the floor of the LAF corridor, but the fixed-rate reverse repo still exists as a definition.)

questions.question_text: The percentage of a bank's Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) that must be kept as cash balance with the RBI is called:
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): SLR is also a percentage of NDTL, but it is held by the bank itself in liquid assets, not as cash with RBI.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: CRR is the share of NDTL that banks must keep as cash with the RBI and it earns no interest. SLR is kept in cash, gold and approved securities with the banks themselves. Memory hook: CRR = Cash with RBI.

questions.question_text: The headquarters of the Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) is located in:
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Most financial institutions such as RBI, NABARD and SEBI are in Mumbai, so students default to Mumbai for SIDBI too.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: SIDBI was set up in 1990 and has its head office in Lucknow. Memory hook: SIDBI = Small bank, Lucknow.

questions.question_text: NABARD was established in 1982 on the recommendation of which committee?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Narasimham Committee is the most famous banking committee (financial sector reforms), so students pick it by default.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Shivaraman Committee (1979) recommended a dedicated apex institution for agriculture and rural credit, leading to NABARD in July 1982. Memory hook: Shivaraman = NABARD.

questions.question_text: In which year were 14 major commercial banks nationalised in India?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): 1980 is the second round of nationalisation (six banks), so students mix up the two rounds.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: On 19 July 1969 the Government nationalised 14 banks having deposits above Rs 50 crore. Six more followed in 1980. Memory hook: 14 banks in 69.

questions.question_text: SEBI was given statutory powers through the SEBI Act passed in which year?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): SEBI was first set up in 1988 as a non-statutory body, so students pick the year of its creation instead of its statutory status.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: SEBI was established administratively in 1988 and became a statutory regulator of the securities market with the SEBI Act, 1992. Memory hook: Set up 88, statutory 92.

questions.question_text: Which institution is known as the 'Banker's Bank' in India?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): SBI is the largest commercial bank, so students think it is the bank for other banks.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: RBI acts as banker to commercial banks by holding their reserves and lending to them as lender of last resort. Memory hook: RBI = Banker to banks and to the Government.

questions.question_text: What is the chemical formula of common salt?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): KCl is potassium chloride, another chloride salt that looks similar to NaCl.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Common salt is sodium chloride (NaCl), formed by neutralisation of NaOH and HCl. Memory hook: Na + Cl = Salt.

questions.question_text: Which cell organelle is called the 'powerhouse of the cell'?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Lysosome is known by another nickname, 'suicide bag', so the two nicknames get swapped.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Mitochondria release energy in the form of ATP during respiration. Ribosomes make proteins. Memory hook: Mitochondria = Energy ATP.

questions.question_text: Which type of mirror is used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles because it gives a wider field of view?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Concave mirrors are used in headlights, shaving mirrors and by dentists, so they are the most common mix-up.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A convex mirror always forms an erect, diminished image and covers a wide area behind the vehicle. Memory hook: Convex = Cars (wide view).

questions.question_text: Deficiency of which vitamin causes the disease scurvy?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets, the other classic bone and tissue disease students mix with scurvy.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency causes scurvy, with bleeding gums and slow wound healing. Vitamin B1 deficiency causes beriberi and Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness. Memory hook: Scurvy = Citrus cure.

questions.question_text: What is the chemical name of baking soda?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Sodium carbonate is washing soda, a close relative of baking soda that students often swap with it.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate (NaHCO3), a mild non-corrosive base used in baking and antacids. Washing soda is Na2CO3.10H2O. Memory hook: Baking soda has Hydrogen (NaHCO3).

questions.question_text: Which part of the human brain is mainly responsible for maintaining posture and balance of the body?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Medulla controls involuntary actions such as heartbeat and breathing, so it is confused with the balance centre.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The cerebellum, in the hindbrain, coordinates voluntary movements, posture and equilibrium. The cerebrum handles thinking and voluntary action. Memory hook: Cerebellum = Coordination and balance.

questions.question_text: When white light passes through a glass prism, which colour deviates the least?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Violet is at the opposite end of the spectrum and deviates the most, so students reverse the order.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Red has the longest wavelength and bends least, while violet has the shortest and bends most. This causes dispersion into VIBGYOR. Memory hook: Red = Rigid (least bending).

questions.question_text: Which chamber of the human heart receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cavae?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Left atrium also receives blood, but it is oxygenated blood coming from the lungs.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The right atrium collects deoxygenated blood from the body and passes it to the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs. Memory hook: Right side = Returned (used) blood.

questions.question_text: Which animal is the national animal of India?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): The lions of the Sarnath capital appear on the national emblem, so students mistake the lion for the national animal.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Bengal tiger (Panthera tigris) is the national animal of India. The lion capital of Ashoka is the national emblem, not an animal designation. Memory hook: Tiger = Animal, Lion = Emblem.

questions.question_text: Who is the author of the book 'The Discovery of India'?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Gandhi's autobiography 'My Experiments with Truth' is far more famous, so he is picked for any freedom-era book.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Nehru wrote The Discovery of India during imprisonment at Ahmednagar Fort (1942 to 1945), and it was published in 1946. Memory hook: Nehru in jail = Discovery of India.

questions.question_text: National Sports Day is observed in India every year on which date, the birth anniversary of hockey player Major Dhyan Chand?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): 12 January is National Youth Day (Swami Vivekananda's birthday), another day linked to youth and activity.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Major Dhyan Chand was born on 29 August 1905, and the day is celebrated as National Sports Day. 14 November is Children's Day. Memory hook: 29 August = Dhyan Chand.

questions.question_text: The term 'Scrum' is associated with which sport?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Polo has its own unusual term, 'chukker', so students link odd team-sport terms with polo.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A scrum is a method of restarting play in rugby, where players from both sides bind together and contest the ball. Memory hook: Scrum = Rugby.

questions.question_text: Who was the first Indian to receive a Nobel Prize?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): C. V. Raman won the first Nobel in Science for an Indian (1930), so students think he came first overall.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Tagore won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913 for Gitanjali. C. V. Raman won the Physics Nobel in 1930. Memory hook: Tagore 1913 = first.

questions.question_text: In which novel by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay did the song 'Vande Mataram' first appear?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Devi Chaudhurani is another Bankim novel with a similar sannyasi-rebellion theme, so it is the closest confusion.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Vande Mataram appears in Anandamath (1882), set around the Sannyasi Rebellion. It was adopted as the national song in 1950. Memory hook: Anandamath = Vande Mataram.

questions.question_text: In which 1967 case did the Supreme Court hold that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368?

options.A: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
options.C: Shankari Prasad v. Union of India
options.D: Minerva Mills v. Union of India

questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Kesavananda Bharati (1973) is the most famous amending-power case, so students pick it even though it came six years later and allowed amendment within the basic structure.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: In Golaknath (1967) the Court held that Fundamental Rights could not be amended. Shankari Prasad (1951) had upheld Parliament's power. Kesavananda (1973) overruled Golaknath and laid down the basic structure doctrine. Memory hook: Golaknath 67 = rights frozen.

questions.question_text: The advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, under which the President may seek its opinion on a question of law or fact of public importance, is provided in which Article?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Article 131 deals with the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in Centre-State disputes, so students mix up the two types of jurisdiction.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 143 lets the President refer a question to the Supreme Court for its opinion, which is not binding on the President. Article 136 is special leave to appeal and Article 142 is enforcement of decrees to do complete justice. Memory hook: 143 = Advice.

questions.question_text: The Ninth Schedule was added to the Constitution by which Amendment?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): The 42nd Amendment (1976) is the best-known big amendment, so students attach every major change to it.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The First Amendment Act, 1951 added the Ninth Schedule to protect land reform laws from court challenge. Memory hook: First Amendment = Ninth Schedule.

questions.question_text: Who decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill or not?

options.C: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
options.D: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha

questions.trap_type: Trap (D): The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is confused with the Speaker because the Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations on Money Bills.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Under Article 110(3), if any question arises whether a Bill is a Money Bill, the decision of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha is final. Memory hook: Money Bill = Speaker's call.

questions.question_text: The limit that the Council of Ministers in a State cannot exceed 15 percent of the total strength of the Legislative Assembly was introduced by which Amendment?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): The 84th Amendment (2001) is close in time and also deals with legislatures (delimitation freeze), so it is easily confused.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The 91st Amendment (2003) capped the size of the Union and State Councils of Ministers at 15 percent of the lower house and tightened the anti-defection law. Memory hook: 91st = 15 percent cap.

questions.question_text: Which Article of the Constitution provides for the establishment of an Inter-State Council?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Article 262 sits right beside it and deals with adjudication of inter-State river water disputes, another inter-State provision.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 263 empowers the President to set up an Inter-State Council to investigate and discuss subjects of common interest between States and the Union. Article 307 relates to an authority for inter-State trade and commerce. Memory hook: 263 = Council for Co-ordination.

questions.question_text: Which was the first Indian state annexed by Lord Dalhousie under the Doctrine of Lapse?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Jhansi is the best-known annexation under the Doctrine of Lapse (1853), so students assume it was the first.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Satara was annexed in 1848, followed by Sambalpur (1849), Jhansi (1853) and Nagpur (1854). Memory hook: Satara = Start of lapse.

questions.question_text: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878, which restricted Indian-language newspapers, was passed during the Viceroyalty of:
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Lord Ripon repealed the Act in 1882, so students link his name with it.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Lord Lytton (1876 to 1880) passed the Vernacular Press Act in 1878, and Ripon repealed it in 1882. Curzon is linked with the Indian Universities Act (1904) and the Partition of Bengal. Memory hook: Lytton = Lock on the press.

questions.question_text: Which of the following was NOT a member of the Cabinet Mission of 1946?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Stafford Cripps is linked mainly with the 1942 Cripps Mission, so students wrongly think he was absent from the 1946 mission.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Cabinet Mission had three British Cabinet ministers: Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A. V. Alexander. Lord Wavell was the Viceroy who worked with them but was not a member. Memory hook: three ministers, Viceroy outside.

questions.question_text: Which Indian state has the longest mainland coastline?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Andhra Pradesh has the second longest coastline and the longest on the east coast, so it is the closest confusion.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Gujarat has the longest coastline among Indian states, followed by Andhra Pradesh. Tamil Nadu is third on the mainland. Memory hook: Gujarat = Great coast.

questions.question_text: Which is the highest peak of Peninsular India?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Doddabetta is the highest peak of the Nilgiri hills and the most visited, so students pick it as the highest overall.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Anamudi (2,695 m) in the Anamalai hills of Kerala is the highest peak of the Western Ghats and Peninsular India. Mullayanagiri is the highest in Karnataka. Memory hook: Anamudi = Peninsular peak.

questions.question_text: The Dhuandhar Falls near Jabalpur are formed by which river?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): The Tapi is the other major west-flowing river of central India, so students swap it with the Narmada.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Narmada plunges over the Dhuandhar Falls at Bhedaghat in Madhya Pradesh, near marble rocks. Memory hook: Dhuandhar = Narmada (smoke cascade).

questions.question_text: Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) were set up in 1975 on the recommendation of which Working Group?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The Shivaraman Committee (1979) also dealt with rural credit but led to NABARD, not the RRBs.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Narasimham Working Group (1975) recommended RRBs, and the first five were set up on 2 October 1975, later governed by the RRB Act, 1976. Memory hook: RRB = Narasimham Working Group, 1975.

questions.question_text: What is the chemical formula of Plaster of Paris?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): CaSO4.2H2O is gypsum, the raw material from which Plaster of Paris is made, so the two hydrates get swapped.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Plaster of Paris is calcium sulphate hemihydrate, made by heating gypsum at about 373 K. It sets into gypsum when mixed with water. Memory hook: Plaster = Half water.

questions.question_text: The twinkling of stars is caused by which phenomenon?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Scattering explains the blue colour of the sky and the red Sun at sunrise, so students apply it to twinkling as well.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Starlight passes through layers of air with changing density and refracts continuously, so the apparent position and brightness of the star keep fluctuating. Planets do not twinkle because they are extended sources. Memory hook: Twinkle = Refraction in moving air.

questions.question_text: Who was the first recipient of the Jnanpith Award, presented for the year 1965?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Tarashankar Bandyopadhyay won the Jnanpith the very next year (1966), so students pick him as the first winner.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Malayalam poet G. Sankara Kurup received the first Jnanpith Award for his collection Odakkuzhal. The award is given by the Bharatiya Jnanpith for literary excellence in Indian languages. Memory hook: First Jnanpith = Kurup, Malayalam.

questions.question_text: Which flower is the national flower of India?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): The rose is the most widely recognised flower in everyday life, so students choose it by default.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The lotus (Nelumbo nucifera) is the national flower of India and symbolises purity and heritage. Memory hook: Lotus grows in mud yet stays pure.

questions.question_text: Which tree is the national tree of India?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The peepal is also a sacred fig tree, so it is the closest confusion with the banyan.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The banyan (Ficus benghalensis) is the national tree of India, noted for its aerial roots and long life. The mango is the national fruit. Memory hook: Banyan = Big and eternal.

questions.question_text: World Environment Day is observed every year on which date?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): 22 April is Earth Day, another environmental day that is often swapped with World Environment Day.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: World Environment Day is observed on 5 June, started by the United Nations in 1972 (first celebrated 1974). 16 September is World Ozone Day and 11 July is World Population Day. Memory hook: June 5 = Environment.

questions.question_text: The term 'Birdie' is associated with which sport?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): The shuttlecock in badminton is also called a 'bird', so students link 'birdie' with badminton.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: In golf, a birdie means completing a hole in one stroke under par. Other golf terms are eagle, bogey and par. Memory hook: Birdie = Golf score.

questions.question_text: Who wrote the ancient Sanskrit work on statecraft, the 'Arthashastra'?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Kalidasa is the most famous classical Sanskrit author, so students attach any Sanskrit text to him.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Arthashastra is attributed to Kautilya (Chanakya), adviser to Chandragupta Maurya, and deals with politics, economy and military strategy. Kalidasa wrote Abhijnanashakuntalam and Panini wrote the Ashtadhyayi (grammar). Memory hook: Arthashastra = Kautilya = economy and state.

questions.question_text: Teachers' Day in India is celebrated on 5 September in honour of the birth anniversary of which person?

options.D: Dr. A. P. J. Abdul Kalam

questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Rajendra Prasad was the first President of India, so students link him with a day honouring a leader of the same era.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, a philosopher and teacher, was born on 5 September 1888 and later became the second President of India. Memory hook: 5 September = Radhakrishnan = Teacher.

questions.question_text: Kuchipudi, a classical dance form of India, originated in which state?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Tamil Nadu is the home of Bharatanatyam, the classical dance most often confused with Kuchipudi.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Kuchipudi takes its name from the village of Kuchipudi in Andhra Pradesh. Odissi comes from Odisha and Kathakali from Kerala. Memory hook: Kuchipudi = Krishna district, Andhra.

questions.question_text: The ancient Tamil epic 'Silappathikaram' was composed by:
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Sattanar wrote Manimekalai, the sequel epic to Silappathikaram, so the two authors are swapped.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Ilango Adigal composed Silappathikaram, the story of Kovalan and Kannagi. Sattanar wrote Manimekalai, Tiruvalluvar wrote the Tirukkural and Kamban wrote the Tamil Ramayana. Memory hook: Ilango = Silappathikaram.

questions.question_text: Who was the first Prime Minister of independent India?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Sardar Patel was the first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, so students confuse the two top offices.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Jawaharlal Nehru took office on 15 August 1947 and served until 1964. Rajendra Prasad was the first President. Memory hook: Nehru = first PM, Prasad = first President.

questions.question_text: The Arjuna Award in India is given for outstanding achievement in which field?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): The Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize is the well-known science award, so students pair national awards with the wrong field.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Arjuna Award, instituted in 1961 by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, recognises outstanding sportspersons. Memory hook: Arjuna = Archer = Athlete.

questions.question_text: Which Vedic text, among the four Vedas, deals mainly with music, melodies and chants?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): The Rigveda is the oldest Veda and contains the hymns that the Samaveda later sets to melody, so the two are confused.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Samaveda is a collection of melodies (saman) largely drawn from the Rigveda and is regarded as the source of Indian classical music. The Yajurveda gives sacrificial formulas and the Atharvaveda contains spells and charms. Memory hook: Sama = Song.

questions.question_text: What is the SI unit of electric current?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Volt is the unit of potential difference, which is closely linked with current in circuit problems.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The ampere (A) is the SI base unit of electric current, equal to a flow of one coulomb of charge per second. Volt measures potential difference, ohm measures resistance and watt measures power. Memory hook: A for Ampere, A for current.

questions.question_text: Which component of human blood is mainly responsible for carrying oxygen?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Plasma is the liquid part of blood that carries many substances, so students think it carries oxygen too.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which binds oxygen and transports it from lungs to tissues. White cells defend the body and platelets help in clotting. Memory hook: Red cells = Respiratory carriers.

questions.question_text: A solution that has a pH value of 7 is:
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Students sometimes treat pure water as slightly basic because it is the 'base' liquid of solutions.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: On the pH scale (0 to 14), 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic and above 7 is basic. Pure water at 25 degrees Celsius has pH 7. Memory hook: Seven = Even (neutral).

questions.question_text: Sound cannot travel through which of the following?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Students think sound needs only 'thin' media like air, forgetting it can travel through solids and liquids but never through empty space.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium of particles to propagate, so it cannot travel through a vacuum. It travels fastest in solids such as steel. Memory hook: No particles, no sound.

questions.question_text: Which gas do plants absorb from the atmosphere for photosynthesis?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Oxygen is the gas that plants release during photosynthesis, so students reverse the direction of exchange.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: In photosynthesis, plants take in carbon dioxide and water, and with sunlight produce glucose and release oxygen. Memory hook: Plants take CO2, give O2.

questions.question_text: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Gallium melts at about 30 degrees Celsius, so students confuse it as liquid at room temperature, but it stays solid at normal room temperature.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at ordinary room temperature, which is why it is used in some thermometers. Memory hook: Mercury = Quicksilver.

questions.question_text: Which mode of heat transfer does not require any material medium?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Convection is also taught alongside radiation, but it needs a moving fluid medium, so students pick it by confusion.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Radiation transfers heat as electromagnetic waves and can travel through a vacuum, as the Sun's heat reaches the Earth. Conduction needs solids and convection needs fluids. Memory hook: Radiation = Ray, no medium.

questions.question_text: Who is regarded as the 'Father of Genetics' for his experiments on pea plants?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Charles Darwin is the best-known biologist, so students attach every biology title to him.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Gregor Mendel, an Austrian monk, worked on pea plants in the 1850s and 1860s and laid down the laws of inheritance. De Vries was one of those who rediscovered his work in 1900. Memory hook: Mendel = Peas.

questions.question_text: The headquarters of the Reserve Bank of India is located in which city?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): RBI was originally headquartered in Calcutta (Kolkata) when it started in 1935, so students pick the old location.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The RBI's central office moved from Kolkata to Mumbai in 1937 and is permanently located there. Memory hook: RBI = Mumbai, Mint Road area.

questions.question_text: Which authority issues currency notes of all denominations except the one-rupee note in India?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The one-rupee note and all coins are issued by the Ministry of Finance, so students confuse it with the issuer of the other notes.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Under Section 22 of the RBI Act, 1934, the RBI has the sole right to issue bank notes in India. The one-rupee note and coins come from the Government of India. Memory hook: RBI = Notes, Finance Ministry = Coins and 1 rupee.

questions.question_text: In banking, what does the abbreviation KYC stand for?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): 'Know Your Credit' sounds plausible because banks check credit history, so it is the closest wrong expansion.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: KYC means Know Your Customer, the process banks follow to verify identity and address of customers to prevent fraud and money laundering. Memory hook: KYC = Know, not Credit.

questions.question_text: The Indian rupee is represented by which symbol, adopted officially in 2010?

options.A: A blend of Devanagari 'Ra' and Roman 'R', with two horizontal lines at the top
options.B: The letter R with one slash
options.C: A Devanagari letter 'Ru' with a dot

questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Many people think the symbol is just a Latin R with a slash, ignoring that it blends Devanagari 'Ra' and Latin R with two parallel bars.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The rupee symbol was designed by D. Udaya Kumar and approved by the Union Cabinet in 2010. It blends the Devanagari letter Ra with the Latin capital R and has two parallel horizontal bars. Memory hook: Two bars = flag, equality.

questions.question_text: A situation in which the general price level in the economy rises continuously over time is called:
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Disinflation is a fall in the rate of inflation (prices still rise), and its name is easily confused with inflation.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, which reduces the purchasing power of money. Deflation is a sustained fall in prices. Memory hook: Inflation = Increase in prices.

questions.question_text: Agriculture and allied activities belong to which sector of the economy?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Agro-processing industries like sugar mills are secondary, which makes students place all agriculture-related work in the secondary sector.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The primary sector extracts natural resources and includes agriculture, fishing, forestry and mining. The secondary sector covers manufacturing and the tertiary sector covers services. Memory hook: Primary = Produce from nature.

questions.question_text: The headquarters of the State Bank of India (SBI) is located in:
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): SBI's ancestor, the Imperial Bank of India, was formed in Calcutta, so students pick Kolkata.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: SBI has its corporate centre at Nariman Point, Mumbai. It traces its roots to the Bank of Calcutta (1806), and the State Bank of India Act was passed in 1955. Memory hook: SBI = Mumbai.

questions.question_text: The Industrial Finance Corporation of India (IFCI), the first development financial institution of India, was set up in which year?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): IDBI was set up in 1964, another major development bank, so its year is confused with IFCI.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: IFCI was established in 1948 under the IFC Act to provide medium and long-term credit to industry. ICICI came in 1955 and IDBI in 1964. Memory hook: IFCI = First, 1948.

questions.question_text: Which type of tax is levied directly on the income of a person and cannot be shifted to someone else?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Students mix up the two categories because both are collected by the Government, but indirect taxes can be passed on to consumers.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A direct tax such as income tax is paid by the person on whom it is levied and the burden is not shifted. Excise and customs duties are indirect taxes. Memory hook: Direct = Directly paid by you.

questions.question_text: India's first Five Year Plan (1951 to 1956) gave the highest priority to which sector, based on the Harrod-Domar model?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The Second Five Year Plan (Mahalanobis model) stressed heavy industry, so students apply it to the first plan.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The First Plan emphasised agriculture, irrigation and power, including projects such as Bhakra Nangal and Hirakud. The Second Plan shifted to heavy industry. Memory hook: First plan = Food first.

questions.question_text: Which is the largest hot desert in the world?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): The Gobi is a large Asian desert, but it is a cold desert, so it is sometimes mistaken as the largest overall.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Sahara in North Africa covers around 9 million sq km and is the largest hot desert. Antarctica is the largest desert overall as a cold desert. Memory hook: Sahara = Super hot.

questions.question_text: Which is the largest state of India by area?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Madhya Pradesh is the second largest state and is the most common wrong pick.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Rajasthan covers about 342,239 sq km and is the largest state in India by area, followed by Madhya Pradesh. Memory hook: Rajasthan = Royal and Really big.

questions.question_text: Which Indian city is known as the 'Pink City'?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Jodhpur is called the 'Blue City', another Rajasthan city nickname linked to a colour.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Jaipur earned the name Pink City from the terracotta-pink buildings of its old walled city, painted in 1876 to welcome the Prince of Wales. Udaipur is the City of Lakes and Jaisalmer the Golden City. Memory hook: Jaipur = Pink.

questions.question_text: The 'Palghat Gap', a major mountain pass, connects which two states across the Western Ghats?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The Western Ghats also pass through Karnataka and Goa, so students pick another Ghat-adjacent state pair.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Palghat Gap lies between the Nilgiri Hills and Anamalai Hills, linking Palakkad in Kerala with Coimbatore in Tamil Nadu. Thal Ghat and Bhor Ghat are passes in Maharashtra. Memory hook: Palghat = Kerala-Tamil Nadu gateway.

questions.question_text: Under the Constitution of India, the Governor of a State is appointed by whom?

options.A: The Chief Justice of the High Court
options.B: The Chief Minister of the State

questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The Chief Minister heads the State government, so students assume the State picks its own Governor.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 155 says the Governor is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal, in practice on the advice of the Union government. The Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President. Memory hook: Governor = President's appointee.

questions.question_text: Superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of elections is vested in the Election Commission under which Article?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Article 326 also sits in the elections Part (adult suffrage as the basis of elections), so it is the closest confusion.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 324 in Part XV vests the Election Commission with control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President. Article 315 is for Public Service Commissions and Article 326 gives adult suffrage. Memory hook: 324 = Election body.

questions.question_text: Article 21A, which makes free and compulsory education a Fundamental Right for children aged 6 to 14 years, was inserted by which Constitutional Amendment?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): The 61st Amendment lowered the voting age to 18, another amendment about citizens' rights, so it gets mixed up.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A, changed Article 45 and added a Fundamental Duty in Article 51A. The Right to Education Act, 2009 later gave effect to Article 21A. Memory hook: 86th = Education right.

questions.question_text: The President can promulgate an Ordinance when Parliament is not in session under which Article of the Constitution?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Article 213 gives the same power to the Governor of a State, so students swap the two.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 123 allows the President to issue Ordinances with the force of law when either House is not in session. They must be laid before Parliament and lapse six weeks after Parliament reassembles unless approved earlier. Memory hook: 123 = President's ordinance, 213 = Governor's ordinance.

questions.question_text: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is appointed by the President under which Article?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Article 149 describes the duties and powers of the CAG, so students pick it for the appointment provision.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 148 provides for the appointment, oath and removal of the CAG, who can be removed only in the same manner as a Supreme Court judge. Article 149 gives duties, 150 the form of accounts and 151 the audit reports. Memory hook: 148 = Appointment, 149 = Audit duties.

questions.question_text: Who built the Red Fort (Lal Qila) in Delhi?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Akbar built the famous Agra Fort, so students credit him with the Delhi fort as well.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Shah Jahan built the Red Fort as part of his new capital Shahjahanabad, between 1639 and 1648. Aurangzeb added the barbican walls later. Memory hook: Shah Jahan = Red Fort and Taj Mahal.

questions.question_text: Which ruler is credited with reorganising the old highway from Sonargaon in Bengal to Peshawar, which later came to be known as the Grand Trunk Road?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Akbar is the best-known Mughal administrator, so students credit him with every major Mughal-era road.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Sher Shah Suri (1540 to 1545) repaired and extended this highway, called Sadak-e-Azam, and built sarais at regular intervals along it. Memory hook: Sher Shah = Sadak-e-Azam.

questions.question_text: Who presided over the first session of the Indian National Congress held at Bombay in 1885?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): A. O. Hume helped found the Congress and was its first General Secretary, so students pick him as president.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee was the first President of the INC at the Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay, with 72 delegates. Dadabhai Naoroji presided in 1886 and Badruddin Tyabji in 1887. Memory hook: 1885 Bombay = Bonnerjee.

questions.question_text: Subhas Chandra Bose was elected President of the Indian National Congress for the first time at which session?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Tripuri (1939) is the session where Bose was re-elected and then resigned, so it is the closest confusion.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Bose presided over the Haripura session in Gujarat in February 1938 and was re-elected in 1939 at Tripuri, defeating Pattabhi Sitaramayya. Faizpur (1936) was presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru. Memory hook: Haripura = first term, Tripuri = second term.

questions.question_text: The Revolt of 1857 broke out as a general uprising on 10 May 1857 at which place?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Barrackpore saw the earlier Mangal Pandey incident in March 1857, so students treat it as the start of the revolt.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: On 10 May 1857, sepoys at Meerut rebelled, freed their jailed comrades and marched to Delhi, where they proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar the leader. Memory hook: Meerut = outbreak, Delhi = capital of the revolt.

questions.question_text: What is the capital of Australia?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Sydney is the largest and best-known Australian city, so it is the usual wrong choice.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Canberra is the purpose-built capital of Australia, planned as a compromise between the rival cities of Sydney and Melbourne. Memory hook: Canberra = Capital, Sydney = Skyline.

questions.question_text: The Hirakud Dam, one of the longest earthen dams in the world, is built across which river?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The Brahmani is another major river of Odisha, so students pick it by state association.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Hirakud Dam near Sambalpur in Odisha is on the Mahanadi and was one of the first major multipurpose projects after Independence. It serves flood control, irrigation and power. Memory hook: Hirakud = Mahanadi.

questions.question_text: The Bosphorus Strait connects the Black Sea with which water body?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The Dardanelles links the Sea of Marmara to the Aegean, so the Aegean is confused with the Bosphorus link.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Bosphorus runs through Istanbul and joins the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara. The Dardanelles then leads from Marmara to the Aegean Sea. Memory hook: Bosphorus = Black to Marmara, Dardanelles = Marmara to Aegean.

questions.question_text: Jim Corbett National Park, the oldest national park of India, established in 1936, is located in which state?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Kaziranga in Assam is the best-known national park, so students assume the oldest one is also there.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Jim Corbett National Park was set up in 1936 as Hailey National Park and lies in Uttarakhand. It was the first area covered under Project Tiger in 1973. Memory hook: Corbett = Uttarakhand, 1936.

questions.question_text: What is the full form of NEFT, the retail electronic payment system operated by the RBI?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): 'Trading' sounds plausible because of electronic stock trading, but the T stands for Transfer.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: NEFT is a nationwide system that lets bank customers transfer funds electronically from any bank branch to another bank's branch. Memory hook: NEFT = National Electronic Funds Transfer.

questions.question_text: How many members does the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) have under the RBI Act, 1934 as amended in 2016?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Students forget that the Governor is a member and chairperson and count only 5.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Section 45ZB provides for six members: the Governor (chairperson), the Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer nominated by the Central Board, and three external members appointed by the Central Government. Memory hook: 3 from RBI + 3 from outside = 6.

questions.question_text: Who was the first Indian to be appointed Governor of the Reserve Bank of India?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Benegal Rama Rau succeeded Deshmukh and was also an Indian Governor, so students pick the wrong one of the two.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Sir Osborne Smith was the first Governor of RBI (1935), and Sir C. D. Deshmukh became the first Indian Governor in 1943. Memory hook: Smith = British first, Deshmukh = Indian first.

questions.question_text: Which authority regulates and develops the insurance industry in India?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): PFRDA regulates pensions, a neighbouring financial regulator, so it is the closest confusion.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) was set up under the IRDA Act, 1999 to regulate and promote the insurance sector. SEBI regulates securities markets. Memory hook: IRDAI = Insurance.

questions.question_text: Which gas is the most abundant in the Earth's atmosphere?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Oxygen is vital for life, so students assume it is the most abundant, but it forms only about 21 percent.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of dry air by volume, followed by oxygen at about 21 percent and argon at about 0.9 percent. Memory hook: 78 percent N2, 21 percent O2.

questions.question_text: Which vitamin is essential for the normal clotting of blood?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Vitamin B12 is also linked to blood (red cell formation and anaemia), so students confuse the two.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Vitamin K helps the liver make clotting factors, so its deficiency leads to delayed clotting and bleeding. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes pernicious anaemia. Memory hook: K = Koagulation.

questions.question_text: In the human pancreas, insulin is secreted by which cells of the Islets of Langerhans?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Alpha cells secrete glucagon, the opposing hormone, so the two cell types are swapped.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Beta cells secrete insulin, which lowers blood glucose, while alpha cells secrete glucagon, which raises it. Acinar cells make digestive enzymes and belong to the exocrine part. Memory hook: Beta = Brings sugar down.

questions.question_text: Malaria is caused by which type of organism?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Dengue and chikungunya are mosquito-borne viral diseases, so students assume malaria is also viral.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium and spread by the female Anopheles mosquito. Typhoid is bacterial and ringworm is fungal. Memory hook: Malaria = Plasmodium = Protozoan.

questions.question_text: Onam, the harvest festival associated with King Mahabali, is celebrated mainly in which state?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Pongal in Tamil Nadu is another southern harvest festival, so students mix the two.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Onam is the state festival of Kerala, celebrated in the Malayalam month of Chingam with flower carpets (pookalam), boat races and a feast called Onasadya. Memory hook: Onam = Kerala, Pongal = Tamil Nadu.

questions.question_text: The Santosh Trophy is associated with which sport?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Many Indian domestic trophies such as the Ranji and Duleep Trophies belong to cricket, so students assume the same here.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Santosh Trophy is the national football championship for state and institutional teams, run by the All India Football Federation. It is named after Maharaja Manmatha Nath Roy Chowdhury of Santosh. Memory hook: Santosh = Soccer.

questions.question_text: The Sanskrit historical play 'Mudrarakshasa', which describes the rise of Chandragupta Maurya through Chanakya's strategy, was written by:
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Shudraka wrote the Sanskrit play Mrichchhakatika, another classical drama, so the playwrights are confused.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Vishakhadatta wrote Mudrarakshasa, a political play in which Chanakya wins over the minister Rakshasa of the Nandas. Kalidasa wrote Abhijnanashakuntalam and Bhasa wrote Svapnavasavadatta. Memory hook: Mudra-rakshasa = Vishakhadatta.

questions.question_text: Who is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?

options.B: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
options.D: The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha

questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha, so students assign the matching role in the other House to the same office.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 64 makes the Vice-President the ex-officio Chairman of the Council of States, and Article 89 repeats this for the Rajya Sabha. The Deputy Chairman is elected by the members and presides only in the Chairman's absence. Memory hook: VP = Rajya Sabha head.

questions.question_text: Which Article of the Directive Principles of State Policy directs the State to endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code for citizens throughout India?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Article 45 is the neighbouring Directive Principle (early childhood care and education), so students pick the adjacent number.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 44 is the only Directive Principle that mentions a Uniform Civil Code. Article 40 deals with village panchayats and Article 48 with organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry. Memory hook: 44 = one law for all.

questions.question_text: The Tenth Schedule, containing the anti-defection provisions, was added to the Constitution by which Amendment?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The 55th Amendment came just a year later (1986), so students choose the neighbouring amendment by year.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Constitution (Fifty-second Amendment) Act, 1985 added the Tenth Schedule and laid down grounds for disqualification of legislators on the ground of defection. Memory hook: 52nd = Tenth Schedule = defection.

questions.question_text: Who presides over a joint sitting of the two Houses of Parliament summoned to resolve a deadlock over an ordinary Bill?

options.B: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
options.C: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha

questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha heads one of the two Houses meeting together, so students assume he shares or takes the chair.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 108 provides for the joint sitting, and Article 118(4) says the Speaker presides, or the Deputy Speaker in the Speaker's absence. The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha never presides over it. Memory hook: Joint sitting = Speaker in the chair.

questions.question_text: The office of the Attorney General of India is provided for under which Article of the Constitution?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Article 165 creates the Advocate General of a State, the parallel State-level law officer, so the two offices are swapped.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 76 empowers the President to appoint as Attorney General a person qualified to be a Supreme Court judge. Article 78 lists the Prime Minister's duties to furnish information to the President, and Article 124 establishes the Supreme Court. Memory hook: 76 = Union law officer, 165 = State law officer.

questions.question_text: Which Mauryan emperor gave up conquest by war and adopted the policy of Dhamma after the Kalinga War?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Bindusara was Ashoka's father and the preceding Mauryan emperor, so students pick the nearest ruler on the family list.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Ashoka fought the Kalinga War around 261 BCE, and his Rock Edict XIII expresses remorse over the suffering it caused. He then promoted Dhamma, a code of moral conduct. Memory hook: Kalinga = Ashoka's turning point.

questions.question_text: The Prayaga Prashasti (Allahabad Pillar Inscription), composed by the court poet Harishena, praises which Gupta ruler?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) is the best-known Gupta king, so students attach every Gupta record to him.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The inscription is engraved on an Ashokan pillar at Prayagraj and lists the conquests, qualities and policies of Samudragupta. Harishena was his court poet. Memory hook: Harishena wrote, Samudragupta was praised.

questions.question_text: Sheikh Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan, a prominent Sufi saint of the thirteenth century, belonged to which silsila?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The Chishti silsila is the best known in India, so students assign most early saints to it.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Bahauddin Zakariya was a leading saint of the Suhrawardi silsila, which was strong in Multan and Sind and kept closer ties with the rulers than the Chishtis did. The Qadiri and Naqshbandi orders became influential in India later. Memory hook: Multan = Suhrawardi.

questions.question_text: Which Governor-General declared the practice of Sati illegal through a regulation passed in 1829?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Lord Canning's term saw the Widow Remarriage Act of 1856, another social reform law, so the two reforms get mixed.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Regulation XVII of 1829, passed under Lord William Bentinck, banned Sati in the Bengal Presidency, with strong support from Raja Rammohan Roy. Memory hook: Bentinck = Banned Sati.

questions.question_text: The Adi Granth, the first compilation of Sikh scripture, was compiled in 1604 by which Guru?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Guru Gobind Singh added the hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur and gave the scripture its final form, so students credit him with the original compilation.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Guru Arjan Dev gathered the hymns of the first five Gurus along with compositions of saints such as Kabir, Ravidas and Baba Farid, and installed the Adi Granth at Harmandir Sahib. Guru Gobind Singh later included Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns. Memory hook: Arjan = Adi Granth, Gobind = final form.

questions.question_text: Which imaginary line passes through Greenwich in London and is taken as 0 degree longitude?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): The Equator is the 0 degree line of latitude, so students confuse the two zero lines.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Prime Meridian passes through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich and divides the Earth into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres. Memory hook: Meridian = longitude, Equator = latitude.

questions.question_text: Which soil, formed from the weathering of volcanic Deccan lava and locally called 'regur', is considered ideal for cotton cultivation?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Alluvial soil is the most widespread and fertile soil in India, so students pick it for every major crop.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Black soil retains moisture, is rich in lime, iron and magnesia, and suits cotton, which is why it is also called black cotton soil. It is found mainly on the Deccan plateau. Memory hook: Regur = Black = Cotton.

questions.question_text: The Nagarjuna Sagar Dam, a major masonry dam in southern India, is built across which river?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): The Tungabhadra is a major tributary of the Krishna with its own well-known dam, so students choose it by association.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Nagarjuna Sagar lies on the border of present-day Telangana and Andhra Pradesh and impounds the Krishna. It supports irrigation and hydropower. Memory hook: Nagarjuna Sagar = Krishna.

questions.question_text: Which pass in the Pir Panjal range links Jammu with the Kashmir Valley?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Zoji La also lies on the Srinagar route, but it connects the Kashmir Valley with Ladakh across the Great Himalaya, not Jammu through the Pir Panjal.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Banihal Pass crosses the Pir Panjal range between Jammu and the Kashmir Valley, and a road tunnel beneath it carries the highway. Khardung La is in Ladakh and Bara-lacha La lies on the Manali-Leh route. Memory hook: Banihal = Jammu to Kashmir, Zoji La = Kashmir to Ladakh.

questions.question_text: A cheque with two parallel lines drawn across its face, usually at the top left corner, is called a:
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): An open cheque is the uncrossed form that can be cashed over the counter, the exact opposite of a crossed cheque.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A crossed cheque can only be credited to the payee's bank account and cannot be encashed over the counter. This makes it safer against theft or loss. Memory hook: Two lines = pay through the bank only.

questions.question_text: The Export-Import Bank of India (EXIM Bank), set up in 1982 to finance foreign trade, has its head office in which city?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): EXIM Bank is a government-owned institution linked to trade policy, so students place its head office in the national capital.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: EXIM Bank was established under the Export-Import Bank of India Act, 1981 and began operations on 1 March 1982. Its head office is in Mumbai. Memory hook: EXIM = Export-Import, Mumbai port city.

questions.question_text: When the RBI buys or sells government securities in the open market to manage liquidity in the banking system, the tool is known as:
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Moral suasion is a qualitative tool in which the RBI persuades banks through advice, so students mix quantitative and qualitative tools.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: In Open Market Operations, purchase of securities injects money into the system and sale of securities absorbs money from it. Moral suasion, margin requirement and selective credit control are qualitative measures. Memory hook: OMO = RBI trades securities.

questions.question_text: The three Annual Plans of 1966-67, 1967-68 and 1968-69, which came between the Third and the Fourth Five Year Plans, are known as the:
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): The Rolling Plan of 1978 to 1980 was another short-term departure from the five-year format, so students link the two.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: After the Third Plan, the Indo-Pakistan war, droughts and a resource crunch led to the Fourth Plan being postponed. Three Annual Plans were followed instead, and this period is called the Plan Holiday. Memory hook: 1966 to 1969 = Plan Holiday.

questions.question_text: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The joule is the unit of work and energy, which is calculated as force multiplied by distance, so students confuse the two.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: One newton is the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s squared. Pascal measures pressure and watt measures power. Memory hook: Newton = Force, Joule = Work.

questions.question_text: Which acid is naturally present in tamarind?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Citric acid is the best-known natural fruit acid, found in lemon and orange, so students apply it to every sour fruit.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Tamarind contains tartaric acid. Oxalic acid is found in tomato and lactic acid in sour milk. Memory hook: Tamarind = Tartaric (both start with T).

questions.question_text: Which is the smallest bone in the human body?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): The incus is another middle-ear ossicle of very similar size, so students pick the wrong one of the three.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The stapes (stirrup) in the middle ear is the smallest bone and passes vibrations from the incus to the inner ear. The malleus and incus are also tiny but larger. Memory hook: Stapes = Smallest, shaped like a stirrup.

questions.question_text: Which of the following diseases is caused by a virus?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Cholera is a water-borne disease often listed with polio under preventable diseases, but it is bacterial.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Polio is caused by the poliovirus. Cholera is caused by Vibrio cholerae, tetanus by Clostridium tetani and typhoid by Salmonella typhi, all bacteria. Memory hook: Polio = Poliovirus.

questions.question_text: Bihu, the festival that marks the Assamese New Year and the harvest seasons, is celebrated in which state?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): West Bengal celebrates its new year, Poila Boishakh, in the same mid-April period, so students mix the two.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Bihu is the main festival of Assam and is celebrated three times a year: Rongali (Bohag) Bihu in April, Bhogali (Magh) Bihu in January and Kongali (Kati) Bihu in October. Memory hook: Bihu = Assam.

questions.question_text: Who was the first recipient of the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, India's highest award in cinema, given for the year 1969?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Prithviraj Kapoor was an early pioneer of Indian cinema and received the award in 1971, so students pick him as the first.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Devika Rani received the first Dadasaheb Phalke Award, followed by B. N. Sircar in 1970. The award was instituted by the Government of India in 1969 to mark the birth centenary of Dadasaheb Phalke. Memory hook: Phalke Award No. 1 = Devika Rani.

questions.question_text: The Thomas Cup is an international team championship for men in which sport?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The Swaythling Cup is the table tennis team trophy, another men's team championship with a similar format, so the two are swapped.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Thomas Cup is the world men's team championship in badminton, and its women's counterpart is the Uber Cup. It is organised by the Badminton World Federation. Memory hook: Thomas = men, Uber = women, both badminton.

questions.question_text: Which Harappan site on Khadir Bet island in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat, is known for its elaborate water conservation system with large reservoirs?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Rakhigarhi is a major Harappan site in Haryana, so students pick it for any question about a large Harappan town.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Dholavira in Kutch had a series of stone-cut reservoirs and channels to store scarce rainwater in an arid setting. It is also known for a monumental inscription of large signs. Memory hook: Dholavira = Drains and Dams in a desert.

questions.question_text: The Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur was built by which Chola ruler?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Rajendra I was Rajaraja I's son and built a similar grand temple at Gangaikonda Cholapuram, so the two are swapped.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Rajaraja I built the Brihadisvara Temple, which was completed around 1010 CE and is dedicated to Shiva. Rajendra I later founded Gangaikonda Cholapuram as his capital. Memory hook: Rajaraja = Raja of Thanjavur.

questions.question_text: Krishnadevaraya, the most celebrated ruler of the Vijayanagara Empire, belonged to which dynasty?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The Sangama dynasty was the first dynasty, founded by Harihara and Bukka, so students attach the empire's most famous ruler to it.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Krishnadevaraya ruled from 1509 to 1529 and belonged to the Tuluva dynasty. The Aravidu dynasty was the last to rule the empire. Memory hook: Tuluva = Triumph of Krishnadevaraya.

questions.question_text: Which Delhi Sultan introduced a system of fixed prices for grain, cloth and other goods, supervised by an officer called Shahna-i-Mandi?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Muhammad bin Tughluq is famous for bold economic experiments such as token currency, so students credit him with market control.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Alauddin Khalji fixed prices and set up regulated markets so that he could maintain a large standing army at low cost. Memory hook: Alauddin = Army needs cheap goods = price control.

questions.question_text: In 1917, Gandhi launched his first satyagraha in India at Champaran in Bihar on behalf of peasants who were forced to grow which crop?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The Ahmedabad mill strike of 1918 involved cotton textile workers, so students link cotton with Gandhi's early campaigns.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: European planters compelled Champaran peasants to grow indigo on a part of their land under the tinkathia system. Gandhi's intervention led to an inquiry and relief for the peasants. Memory hook: Champaran = Indigo.

questions.question_text: Which of the following UNESCO World Heritage Sites is located in Odisha?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Khajuraho is also famous for temple sculpture, so students confuse it with the sculpted Konark temple.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Sun Temple at Konark was built in the thirteenth century in the form of a giant chariot of the Sun God and was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1984. Khajuraho is in Madhya Pradesh, Hampi in Karnataka and Ellora in Maharashtra. Memory hook: Konark = Chariot of the Sun.

questions.question_text: Lavani, a folk dance form known for its quick rhythm and dholki accompaniment, belongs to which state?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Gujarat is known for the energetic Garba and Dandiya, the best-known western Indian dance forms, so it is the usual wrong pick.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Lavani is a traditional song and dance form of Maharashtra, performed to the beat of the dholki. Garba and Dandiya belong to Gujarat. Memory hook: Lavani = Maharashtra's dholki dance.

questions.question_text: The musician Ustad Bismillah Khan is associated with which musical instrument?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): The sitar is the most famous Hindustani instrument and is linked with Pandit Ravi Shankar, so students choose it by default.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Bismillah Khan raised the shehnai, a wind instrument traditionally played at temples and weddings, to the concert stage. Santoor is linked with Pandit Shivkumar Sharma and sarod with Ustad Amjad Ali Khan. Memory hook: Bismillah = Blowing shehnai.

questions.question_text: The International Court of Justice, the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, has its seat in which city?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Geneva hosts many UN agencies such as the WHO and the ILO, so it is the default guess for UN bodies.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The ICJ sits at the Peace Palace in The Hague, Netherlands. It is the only principal organ of the United Nations that is not located in New York. Memory hook: ICJ = Justice in The Hague.

questions.question_text: Which poet's Sanskrit work 'Gita Govinda', describing the love of Radha and Krishna, is a principal literary source for Odissi dance?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): Vidyapati wrote Radha-Krishna love songs in Maithili, so students link him with the same theme.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Jayadeva composed the Gita Govinda in the twelfth century, and its verses are widely used for abhinaya in Odissi. Memory hook: Jayadeva = Gita Govinda = Odissi.

questions.question_text: On whose recommendations were the Fundamental Duties incorporated in the Constitution of India?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The Sarkaria Commission is the best-known commission linked with the Constitution (Centre-State relations), so students pick it by default.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Swaran Singh Committee was set up during the Emergency to suggest constitutional changes and recommended the inclusion of Fundamental Duties, which Parliament adopted soon after. Balwant Rai Mehta and Ashok Mehta both dealt with Panchayati Raj. Memory hook: Swaran Singh = Duties.

questions.question_text: Which Article of the Directive Principles of State Policy directs the State to take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Article 49 deals with protection of monuments and sits right before Article 50, so students pick the adjacent number.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 50 aims to secure the independence of the judiciary by separating it from the executive in public services. Article 47 deals with nutrition and public health and Article 51 with promotion of international peace and security. Memory hook: 50 = Judges free from executive.

questions.question_text: Which Article of the Constitution provides for a State Election Commission to conduct elections to the Panchayats?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Article 243I provides for the State Finance Commission and sits just before Article 243K, so students pick the adjacent letter.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 243K in Part IX vests the superintendence of Panchayat elections in a State Election Commission headed by a State Election Commissioner appointed by the Governor. Article 243D deals with reservation of seats and 243G with powers and responsibilities of Panchayats. Memory hook: 243K = Keeper of local elections.

questions.question_text: The National Human Rights Commission of India is a statutory body established under which Act?
questions.trap_type: Trap (D): The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 created another statutory grievance body, so students pick it by association.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The NHRC was constituted under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 and is a statutory, not a constitutional, body. Memory hook: NHRC = 1993 Act, statutory.

questions.question_text: Which crop is known as the 'Golden Fibre' of India?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): Cotton is the most important fibre crop of India, so students pick it for any fibre question.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Jute is called the Golden Fibre because of its colour and its importance in making bags, sacks and ropes. It grows well in the fertile flood plains with a hot and humid climate. Memory hook: Jute = Golden fibre for gunny bags.

questions.question_text: Which soil, formed by intense leaching under heavy rainfall and high temperature, is suited to crops such as tea, coffee and cashew nut?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Red soil is also a tropical soil rich in iron, so students pick it, but it forms in areas of low rainfall.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Laterite soil forms where heavy rain washes away nutrients such as lime and silica, leaving iron and aluminium compounds. It needs manure and fertiliser for good yields. Memory hook: Laterite = Leaching.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a tributary of the Godavari river?
questions.trap_type: Trap (C): The Tungabhadra is the best-known peninsular tributary, but it joins the Krishna, not the Godavari.
